## The question

In a fantasy basketball snake draft, twelve managers take turns picking real NBA
players, and each week a team scores points from its starters' box scores. Most
managers draft from a cheat sheet ranked by last season's totals. I wanted to know
whether a model could do measurably better than that, using only information
available before the season starts - and how to prove it without fooling myself.

## Data and cleaning

Sixteen seasons of per-game player logs (2010-11 to 2025-26, about 26,000 rows a
season) from the NBA.com stats API via `nba_api`, plus team rosters for positions
and player bios for age. Each season is cached to Parquet, so the API is called
once.

Most of the work was making the data honest about who was actually available:

**Absence is data, but only after a player arrives.** A season a player missed
entirely is a durability signal. Without it, an early version drafted retired
players who went on to score nothing. So the games-played model fills missed
seasons with zero games - but only from each player's first appearance, or it
penalises sophomores for seasons before they were in the league.

**Missing positions are counted, never dropped.** 208 board players had no
position in the roster data. They are scored against an overall baseline and the
count is reported each run, rather than quietly disappearing.

**The schema is verified, not assumed.** Column names were taken from a real pull
and are validated on every load, so a silent API change fails loudly.

[View the code on GitHub](https://github.com/tlabagala/NBA-Fantasy-Draft)

## Method, and why this one

The project was built in versions, each kept only if it beat the one below it:

- **Projection.** Start with last season's total, then try a per-game rate times
  projected games played, an aging curve, and shrinkage toward a positional mean.
- **Board.** Value over replacement, so a scarce centre outranks an equally good
  guard.
- **Draft engine.** Only starters score, so a roster is worth its best legal
  starting lineup, not the sum of all 13 players. The engine picks whoever adds
  most to *my* lineup, plus a penalty for positions about to run dry before my next
  turn. A greedy draft ignores this and wastes picks on depth it can never start.

The naive "last season's totals" draft is the baseline, not a random draft.
Beating random by 153% shows only that the code is wired up - nobody drafts
randomly.

> The first backtest gave every team the same board, so upgrading the board
> upgraded the whole league and my edge cancelled out. Holding the other eleven
> teams fixed is what made the effect measurable.

Every projection for season N uses only seasons before N. This is enforced by an
assertion in the code and a test that forces it to fail, not left to convention.

## Findings

With the other eleven teams drafting naively and only my strategy changing,
averaged over all twelve draft positions, the engine on the aging-curve board beat
the naive draft by **14.6%** in starting-lineup points. It won all 13 held-out
seasons (2013-14 to 2025-26) and 85% of the 156 slot-seasons.

::: {.column-page}
![Fig 1. The draft engine is the only component that beats naive drafting on its own - and the better aging-curve board nearly doubles its edge, from +7.8% to +14.6%.](../assets/figures/nba-head-to-head.png){.figure-wide}
:::

Two results surprised me. Drafting straight down the value-over-replacement board
was **11.8% worse** than naive: it inflated centres, so in 2023-24 it took Embiid
and Vucevic while Doncic sat on the board. Scarcity only helps inside the engine, which asks
what a player adds to my lineup. And the better projection was worth nothing as a
ranking on its own (-1.4%), but compounded through the engine.

Getting a number I trust took more work on the *test* than on the model:

::: {.column-page}
![Fig 2. Measured with every team on the same board, the engine shows no edge at all (-0.2%); holding the opponents fixed reveals a clear one (+7.8%).](../assets/figures/nba-measurement.png){.figure-wide}
:::

On projection accuracy, last season's total proved hard to beat. Only the aging
curve improved it (mean absolute error 501.8 vs 508.9 points over 13 seasons) and
it cut the systematic over-prediction from +34.9 to +9.1 points per player.
Shrinkage made every metric worse and was switched off. Even so, only 53-58% of
each board's projected first-rounders actually finish in the real top twelve.

## Assumptions and limitations

- **Opponents are simple bots.** The other eleven teams draft greedily and never
  react to my picks. Real managers are smarter, so +14.6% is an upper bound, not a
  forecast.
- **The league settings are placeholders.** Scoring and roster slots are a
  standard Yahoo-style setup until the Yahoo API connection is authorised, so the
  result is for a typical league, not a specific one.
- **Lineups are scored with hindsight by default.** Starters are picked using
  actual totals. Re-scoring with lineups chosen from the projection instead gives
  +15.0%, so the conclusion does not depend on this.
- **Thirteen seasons is a small sample.** After averaging the 12 draft slots,
  each season is one result, and the seasons are treated as independent. That is
  enough to separate +14.6% from zero (95% CI 9.0% to 20.3%) but not to pin down
  its size, and two COVID-shortened seasons add noise.
- **The aging curve has survivorship bias.** It only sees players who lasted
  another season, so late-career decline is understated.
- **No rookies, no bench value.** Players with no NBA history are absent, and
  in-season moves like streaming and trades - where leagues are usually won - are
  not modelled.

What this does not license: a claim that the tool wins leagues. The draft is only
a modest lever in head-to-head fantasy. What it does show is a decision rule that
reliably beats the cheat sheet most managers use.

## Reproducing this

Written in Python with `pandas`, `nba_api`, `plotnine` and `pytest`, with a
Streamlit app for draft day. The 72 tests run offline in seconds. A full backtest
needs about 10 minutes of one-off API pulls. The
[code repo](https://github.com/tlabagala/NBA-Fantasy-Draft) README lists every
result table.
